title: The Average Student Never Existed: Two Growth Curves, One Classroom
author: Samantha Lippert
summary: Third-grade teacher Samantha Lippert documents a year of instructional innovation in a co-taught inclusion classroom (85% economically disadvantaged) where integrated systems for fluency, vocabulary, oral language, and comprehension produced growth significantly above national norms for both populations. Her twelve general education students averaged 193% of expected i-Ready annual reading growth and 1.3x typical oral reading fluency growth; her five SPED students averaged 110% of expected annual growth--defying the Matthew Effect by developing comprehension faster than decoding. Lippert's integrated system included: custom fluency passages embedding core vocabulary in context, Sean Morrissey's word-mapping approach (vocabulary taught in pairs for double exposure), turn-and-talk discourse structures with assigned partners and cold calling after rehearsal, Writing Revolution sentence-level practice, and small-group custom passages matched to assessment-text genre and length. Her central argument: the combined classroom average (165% of expected growth) looked unremarkable, masking two entirely different growth stories--and the average student in that room never actually existed.
points: * General education students averaged 193% of expected i-Ready annual reading growth; SPED students averaged 110%--both exceeded national norms, with SPED students defying the Matthew Effect by developing comprehension faster than decoding. * Custom fluency passages embedded core vocabulary in context, creating multiple daily reps across fluency, comprehension, and writing--making vocabulary exposure pervasive rather than isolated on worksheets. * Turn-and-talk with assigned sentence stems and partner order (decided by seating) ensured every student rehearsed an answer before cold calling, equalizing participation and reducing cognitive pressure for vulnerable students. * Small-group instruction used custom passages matched to the genre and topic of core anchor texts, so background knowledge was built before students encountered complex texts--freeing class time for deeper thinking. * The classroom average masked two entirely different growth stories; the average student in that room never actually existed--a caution against using aggregate data to evaluate classroom outcomes.
quotes: It was my SPED-identified students - the ones you'd expect to need the asterisk - who truly showed me what 'growth' actually means, once I stopped measuring them against the wrong chart entirely.

The more effortless decoding becomes for students, the more working memory the students have left over for actually thinking about meaning. A kid still sounding out words doesn't have much left in the tank for comprehension.
I believe that predictable routines free up bandwidth - when the shape of the lesson is already known, kids spend less energy on logistics and more of it on content.

The average student in that room never actually existed. Underneath that average were two very different growth stories: one group performing well above grade level and continuing to accelerate, and another group making meaningful gains while still working toward foundational reading skills.
Growth and proficiency are not competing answers. They're answers to different questions. One asks, 'How far did students move?' The other asks, 'Where did they end up?' You need both.
